content: Requirements and privacy analysts need SPRAT, a collaborative workbench for aligning web-system requirements with privacy and security policies. Users should be able to capture goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and legal-compliance information; trace goals back to their source policies; organize them with flexible classifications; and compare analyses produced by different people. Access should vary for administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests.

The main outcome is that analysts can produce a clear, traceable set of requirements that shows how web-system features line up with security and privacy obligations. In practice, that means we can point from a requirement or goal back to the source policy or legal rule, and we can see that nothing important was missed.
It would be meeting expectations if different people can independently build analyses and then compare them without losing the reasoning behind decisions. Another practical sign is that the workbench helps us catch gaps or conflicts early, before the requirements move forward into implementation or review.

We need it to handle privacy laws, security policies, internal governance rules, and sometimes project-specific compliance obligations, depending on the system being analyzed. In our context that could include external legal requirements, company standards, and any mandated controls that the analysts have to map to the requirements.
Those sources shape the work by forcing analysts to record where each requirement came from, what part of the rule it satisfies, and any assumptions or exceptions. They also affect how we document things like scenarios and goals, because the traceability has to be strong enough for review, audit, and comparison across analysts.

In practice, a goal is the business or system objective, like protecting customer data or making a service usable under certain constraints. A policy is the rule or obligation we have to follow, usually coming from law, corporate standards, or security guidance, and a requirement is the specific statement we write so the system can meet that goal and comply with that policy.
Typically, people start from a policy or a business need, then derive goals and turn those into requirements during analysis. The distinction matters because we need to show that a requirement is not just a nice idea, but something justified by a goal and anchored to a real policy source.

We need the workbench to show which requirement supports which goal, and which policy or legal source justified that goal or requirement. In many cases one requirement will map to several goals, and one policy will drive many requirements, so the tool has to represent those many-to-many relationships cleanly.
It’s also important to capture overlaps and dependencies, because analysts often reuse the same policy interpretation across different parts of the analysis. If a requirement was derived through another requirement or a scenario, that connection should be visible too so someone reviewing it can understand the reasoning, not just the final statement.

It has to work in a collaborative review setting, often with multiple analysts working on the same project but not necessarily at the same time. We also need it to work when people are comparing their own analysis with someone else’s, or when a project manager or guest is reviewing progress without being able to edit everything.
The main constraints are access control and organizational context, since different roles should see and do different things, and some projects will involve sensitive policy or legal material. I’d also expect it to be usable in a normal office or remote working setup, so people can get to it through the web without special tooling.

People would expect it to be available during normal working hours at least, and realistically close to always on because analysis work is often spread across teams and time zones. If it goes down briefly, that’s tolerable as long as people don’t lose their current work and can pick up again quickly.
What would be disruptive is losing edits, having the comparison data corrupted, or being unable to review policy traceability when a deadline is close. Slowdowns are acceptable if they’re minor, but if search, trace navigation, or saving analyses becomes noticeably sluggish, that would interfere with the day-to-day workflow.

I’d expect a modest but steady level of concurrent use, probably a few dozen people at once across projects, not hundreds in one analysis. The dataset size can still get fairly large because each project can accumulate many goals, scenarios, policies, and requirements, especially if there are multiple analysts contributing versions.
So responsiveness matters more than raw scale. Even if the number of users is moderate, the tool still needs to stay quick when someone is loading a dense analysis, tracing links, or comparing two people’s outputs.

The main goal is to help analysts produce requirements that are clearly aligned with security and privacy obligations, instead of each person interpreting the policies differently. We want reviewers to be able to see that alignment quickly and trust the analysis, even when it was produced by different people.
So in practice SPRAT should reduce ambiguity, make the rationale visible, and help the team converge on a defensible set of requirements.

We’d expect it to be used very early, during requirements and analysis work, before design is finalized. That’s when people are identifying goals, mapping policies, and shaping the initial requirements set.
Later on, it would still be useful during review, change impact analysis, and compliance checks, but probably less for day-to-day implementation work. If a project is closed or fully handed over, usage would likely taper off except for audits or lessons learned.

For day one, the core scenarios are capturing goals, policies, scenarios, and requirements; linking them together so the rationale is traceable; and letting people compare two analyses side by side. We also need the basic role-based access so administrators, project managers, analysts, and guests can each do the right level of work.
What can wait are the nicer workflow features, automation, and deeper reporting. The first release has to prove that teams can organize the analysis, review it, and trust the traceability without needing extra bells and whistles.

They need to see where goals, policies, and requirements match, where they differ, and where one analysis has something the other does not. It’s also important to spot when two people traced the same requirement back to different source policies, because that tells reviewers there’s a disagreement to resolve.
I don’t think there’s a hard rule that only certain analyses can be compared, but it should make sense within the same project or at least the same policy context. Comparing unrelated analyses probably wouldn’t be useful.

At a minimum, each item needs a clear title or name and a description so people know what it is and why it exists. For requirements and policies, we’d also want source or justification information, and for scenarios we’d expect the actor, trigger, and outcome to be captured somehow.
I’m not sure we’ve fully nailed down special validation rules yet, but I’d expect the tool to require trace links where a requirement claims to come from a policy, and to flag missing or inconsistent classifications rather than silently accepting them.

We’d expect it to be reliable in checking the structural consistency of the analysis, like whether links exist, whether classifications are used properly, and whether obvious trace gaps are present. It doesn’t need to make the expert judgment for the analyst, but it should catch mistakes that would undermine review confidence.
So I’d think of it as a strong assistant for validation, not an authority that decides the content is semantically correct. If something looks questionable, it should flag it clearly and let the analyst or reviewer decide.

It should capture the specific source policy reference, the exact part of the policy that justifies the goal, and a short rationale explaining the connection. It’s also useful to record who made the trace and when, so reviewers can see whether it was added deliberately and by whom.
Yes, sometimes the trace won’t be to a single policy line. A goal may be supported by several policies together, or the link may be indirect through a requirement or scenario, so the tool should allow that as long as the relationship is still explainable.

The main scenario is that teams already have analysis work in documents, spreadsheets, or other tools, and they need a practical way to bring the important parts into SPRAT without starting from scratch. The key outcome is preserving the traceability and context of what they already know, so the migrated work is still trustworthy and reviewable.
For scope, I’d focus first on getting the core content and links across cleanly, even if some formatting or historical clutter is left behind. The transition should support a gradual move rather than forcing a big-bang cutover.

It should support situations where a project changes its classification scheme, a policy gets revised, or access rights shift because someone’s role changes. In those cases, past analysis work still needs to be readable as it was at the time it was created, while new work follows the updated rules.
So the important behavior is keeping versioned history or at least clear provenance, rather than rewriting old decisions in a way that makes reviews confusing. People should be able to see what changed, when it changed, and which analyses were affected.

Usually the project manager or administrator would make the update, but I’d expect approval to come from whoever is designated as the policy or governance owner for that project. If the ownership is unclear, the tool shouldn’t let the change go through silently; it should flag it for review and keep the request pending until someone with authority confirms it.
If the responsible person is temporarily unavailable, I’d want a fallback process so work doesn’t stall completely, but that fallback should be explicit and auditable.

We’d need a basic audit trail that shows what changed, who changed it, and when it changed. It should also record the previous version or at least enough detail to reconstruct the earlier state, especially for goals, requirements, policies, and traces.
For impacted analyses, it would help if the tool can show which downstream items were derived from the changed artifact or were reviewed against it, so reviewers can judge whether those earlier analyses are still valid. The main point is to preserve the original context rather than overwrite it.

A few dozen concurrent users is probably fine for normal use, but it could still be a problem during heavy collaborative sessions when several people are editing, tracing, and reviewing the same project at once. Large imports or bulk updates could also create temporary slowdowns, especially if they trigger trace recalculation or permission checks.
Cross-project reviews are another case where responsiveness matters, because people may be comparing many artifacts at the same time. So I’d want special handling for those bursts, even if the average user count stays modest.

I’d record the concurrent user level as a tentative assumption for now. We don’t have a firm number beyond “a few dozen,” and I’d rather avoid locking in a limit that we haven’t validated with the teams.

Yes, the tool should make overlapping traces visible rather than hiding them under a single path. If an item belongs to multiple paths, it should show all of the relevant links and make it clear which one is primary if the team has chosen to designate one.
The business rule I’d expect is that nothing gets lost just because it appears in more than one analysis route. It should be easy to see shared dependencies, and reviewers should be able to understand the overlap without confusion.

Yes, for sensitive projects I’d expect tighter access controls, especially for guests and analysts who are not assigned to that project. In some cases, access might need to be limited to approved devices or trusted networks, but I’m not sure we want to make that a universal rule across all projects.
If there’s any location or device restriction, it should probably be driven by the project’s sensitivity and the administrator’s policy, with extra approval only for the most restricted material.

We should note that as tentative for now. I think the general idea is clear, but the exact conditions and fallback rules will depend on the security policy for each project and we haven’t pinned those down yet.

The derived-from link should stay visible even if the source item is later revised or marked inactive, because people still need to understand where the requirement came from. It should be able to chain through multiple levels when that history matters, but the UI should still make the direct parent clear so the trail isn’t ambiguous.
I’d treat derived links differently from direct goal or policy traces, since they mean a different kind of relationship. The direct trace is more about justification or compliance, while derived-from is more about lineage.

It should preserve the intermediate goals or policy versions when that helps explain the justification path. Just showing the most direct policy link would be too thin for reviewers who need to understand why the requirement exists.
At the same time, the direct policy link should still be prominent so people can quickly get to the authoritative source.

New analysts should be able to get started with basic capture and trace tasks with minimal guidance, like entering goals, scenarios, and linking a requirement to its source. We’d expect the more advanced classification and comparison features to need a bit more onboarding.
If there are exceptions, they’d mostly be for very sensitive projects or complicated policy sets, where we’d want extra support and clearer guidance from an administrator or project manager.

Yes, in sensitive projects I would expect some of those actions to be limited. A new analyst might be able to draft entries, but not finalize or publish traces without a project manager or more experienced analyst reviewing them first.
For lower-risk projects, though, I’d want the workflow to stay lightweight so they can do the basic capture and trace work without a lot of approval friction.

In low-risk projects, those basic capture tasks should mostly remain self-service once they’ve learned the workflow. I’d still keep final approval or anything that changes official compliance wording behind a more senior role, but simple editing, reclassifying, and linking to ordinary source types should be open.
If a source type is especially sensitive, like a legal interpretation or a policy exception, that might still need a review step even in a low-risk project.

Project managers should be able to review, comment, compare analyses, and check traceability, but they shouldn’t have unrestricted editing unless that’s part of their role on the project. Guests should be read-only, so they can view approved materials and maybe compare published analyses if allowed, but not change anything or see restricted details.
I’d also block guests from viewing sensitive notes, draft legal-compliance information, and any unapproved trace links unless the project owner explicitly grants access.

Yes, for sensitive projects we’d want location and device to matter. Ideally access would be allowed only from approved corporate networks or trusted devices, and remote access would need stronger authentication and maybe an explicit approval for especially sensitive work.
For urgent situations, I think there should be an exception process rather than a blanket block, because people do sometimes need access while traveling or responding off-hours. That exception should be logged and time-limited.

For very sensitive projects or complex policy sets, I’d want guided setup, examples of acceptable classifications, and probably a short review by an administrator or project manager before the work is considered ready. It would also help to have inline explanations for how comparisons are interpreted, since people can draw the wrong conclusions if the policy language is subtle.
I’d skip or reduce those extra steps only when the project is already using a standard template or the analyst has proven experience with that exact policy domain. In that case, the system should let them move faster without losing the audit trail.

We’d definitely need at least a structured machine-readable export, like CSV or JSON, and a human-readable one like PDF or Word for reviews and reporting. I’d also want exports to preserve trace links and audit metadata, not just the final text.
Certain formats should be restricted if they expose sensitive comments or legal notes, and raw exports should probably be limited to authorized roles. For external sharing, a redacted or approved version should be required rather than an unfiltered export.

If the export includes personal data, legal interpretations, unresolved disputes, or security weaknesses, it should either be redacted or blocked depending on how sensitive it is. Anything that could identify individuals or expose a control gap would usually need explicit approval before release, even if it can be shared at all.
If it’s just a summary of approved, non-sensitive analysis, then a redacted external version should be fine without a lot of extra process.

Yes, role should absolutely affect it. Analysts and project managers can usually generate the full internal exports, while guests should only be able to access approved, redacted versions if they get export access at all. Administrators would have the broadest access, especially for audit or compliance purposes.
The level of detail should drop automatically for lower roles, so things like draft comments, sensitive source links, and personal data are excluded. In some cases, the role should block export entirely if the user is trying to pull something classified above their clearance or outside their project scope.

We’d migrate first the active projects, the authoritative source documents, and anything needed to maintain traceability for current work. Older drafts, duplicates, and reference material that isn’t being used right now can stay in the old tools for a while, especially if moving them would create confusion.
Anything sensitive or messy enough that it needs cleanup before import should probably be held back until someone validates it. The main rule is to bring in what people need to work on immediately, not every historical artifact on day one.

I’d treat it as a tentative guideline for now, not a firm rule. We know the active and authoritative materials should come first, but I wouldn’t want to lock that down until we’ve seen a few real projects and how much cleanup or exception handling is actually needed.
If we make it too rigid too early, we’ll probably end up forcing bad imports or slowing the rollout. Better to keep it flexible and confirm the edge cases with the team once we’ve tested the process.

For the first release, I’d keep the should-have set to the core collaboration and traceability functions: capturing goals, scenarios, policies, requirements, and compliance notes; linking them together; classifying them flexibly; and comparing analyses from different people. Basic access control by role is also part of that, because without it the rest doesn’t really hold up.
A capability should stay out of that category if it adds a lot of complexity, depends on external systems we’re not ready to integrate, or mainly serves a niche workflow. If it would delay the first usable version or create more risk than value, I’d treat it as a later enhancement.

I’d keep things like deep workflow automation, advanced analytics dashboards, and tight integration with every possible document repository out of the first release. Those tend to introduce a lot of complexity and usually depend on decisions or systems we haven’t standardized yet.
The main exception would be if one of those is essential for a pilot customer or for meeting a compliance obligation we can’t otherwise satisfy. In that case, I’d consider including just the smallest workable version, but only if it doesn’t compromise the core collaboration features.

A practical test would be whether the pilot or compliance need can still be met without it using the normal SPRAT workflow. If the answer is no, and there’s a real deadline or contractual expectation behind it, then it’s probably essential rather than just nice to have.
The smallest acceptable version should do only the one necessary thing, with no extra automation or broad integration. It has to fit inside the same capture, trace, and compare flow without breaking access control, redaction, or the ability to review and revise analyses.

The boundary should be whether it directly supports the specific pilot or compliance outcome we’re trying to meet. If a feature starts serving additional teams, extra document types, or broader reporting beyond that need, it’s probably past the minimal line.
I’d keep it limited to the smallest path that gets the required result and can be explained and tested against that one obligation. Once we start adding convenience or future-proofing, we’ve moved beyond essential.

The practical rule should be that anything needed to prove or understand the trace link has to come with it, so the policy source, the specific obligation reference, and the current supporting notes or evidence should migrate together. If a linked item is only historical context, duplicated elsewhere, or not needed to explain the current requirement, it can stay behind for later cleanup.
I’d also keep out anything that can’t be verified quickly, because pulling in uncertain links would create more confusion than value during rollout. The goal is to preserve the chain of reasoning for active work, not to import every related artifact immediately.

If the normal workflow can technically do it but not in time or at the required rigor, I’d treat that as an exception only when there’s a hard external deadline, a mandatory access rule, or an evidence standard that the pilot contract explicitly requires. In that case, it should be allowed, but only with a temporary workaround and clear ownership so we can later bring it back into the standard workflow.
If it’s just more convenient or helps reduce manual effort, I wouldn’t call that essential. The bar should be that missing it would cause us to fail the pilot or fall short of the compliance obligation, not just make the team slower.

The owner should be the person accountable for the pilot or compliance outcome, usually the project manager or lead analyst, not a generic support role. It should be tracked as a time-bounded exception inside SPRAT with the reason, the workaround used, and the target date or condition for closing it.
It moves back into the standard workflow when the deadline is met, the required integration becomes available, or the compliance evidence has been formally accepted. If none of those happen, we’d need to review it rather than letting it sit indefinitely.

The practical rule should be whether the capability is strictly necessary to keep an existing analysis process usable on day one. If analysts cannot migrate their current work, open it, trace it, or compare it without that function, then it can be included in minimal form; otherwise it stays out.
I’d still keep the minimal form as narrow as possible and tied to the current process, not to future improvements or nicer-than-before behavior.

The rule should be based on risk and novelty. If the classification is high sensitivity, new to the project, or has unclear handling rules, then guided setup and a short review should be required; if it’s a well-known classification with an approved template and an experienced analyst is using it, they can proceed with minimal help.
I’d also treat anything that affects access control, legal compliance, or redaction as needing the extra review, even if the analyst is experienced. The idea is to prevent mistakes where the consequences would be hard to undo.

Users should be allowed to take the fast path when the action is routine, low risk, and based on an approved template or previously validated pattern. They can skip extra steps if the system still captures who did it, what changed, when it happened, and which source policy or requirement it came from.
If the action affects sensitive classifications, legal compliance, access permissions, or a new trace link, I wouldn’t allow skipping the extra steps. Traceability has to stay intact even when we reduce friction.

It should stop as soon as the original blocker is gone, meaning the deadline has passed, the missing integration is live, or the acceptance evidence has been approved and archived. At that point, continuing the workaround just adds risk and makes the record harder to trust.
If the blocker is only partially resolved, I’d keep the workaround only until the team confirms the standard path is workable again. If there’s any uncertainty, it should be reviewed rather than automatically extended.

If an artifact naturally belongs in more than one view, like a requirement that is both security-related and tied to a legal obligation, it should be allowed multiple classifications. Reclassification later should be allowed when the analyst is refining the analysis or correcting an early placeholder, as long as the history is preserved.
A single locked classification makes sense only when changing it would break established trace links, access rules, or compliance reporting. In those cases, the system should force a deliberate review rather than letting it drift.

The review should check whether the proposed change would break any existing traceability, alter who can see or edit the artifact, or invalidate any compliance evidence already attached to it. It should also confirm that any dependent goals, requirements, or policies have been updated so nothing is left inconsistent.
If those impacts can’t be fully accounted for, then the classification should stay locked. The approval should only happen when the downstream effects are understood and recorded.

There should be a very narrow exception for obvious corrections, like fixing a spelling mistake or reverting an accidental misclick that doesn’t change meaning or visibility. In those cases, the system could apply the change immediately, but it still needs to log the before and after values and who made the change.
Anything that could alter traceability, access, or compliance evidence should go through review first. If there’s any doubt about impact, I’d treat it as review required.
